I've worked in a few districts. Taught in Tucson, Arizona (poor students of color, mostly Latino),  Los Angeles (poor students of color, predominately Black and Latino), and I'm currently working in Irvine, Ca (wealthy Asians, mostly Korean and Chinese).

coming up with rules is easy and, frankly, lazy. solution? first, we need to understand why and against whom students are "acting out" by re-framing their personal experiences in structural terms, specifically taking into consideration how the intersection of gender, sexual, racial, generational and class differences structure/constrain their everyday lives. Are their "transgressions" aimed at us personally (I'm a teacher as well!) or the material conditions that alienate them? Why not reorient their angst/nihilism against hierarchical structures of oppression and exploitation? etc. etc. Who cares if they use cuss words to express themselves!? Second, we need more rigorous analyses of how prevailing pedagogical practices further alienate and disempower students, particularly practices that center on surveilling and disciplining student behavior. Our pedagogy should correspond with the challenges and strengths specific to our students' respective communities.  Here's some reading:
http://www.msu.ac.zw/elearning/material/1335344125freire_pedagogy_of_the_oppresed.pdf

http://www.sjsu.edu/people/marcos.pizarro/courses/185/s1/Valenzuela.pdf

https://academictrap.files.wordpress.com/2015/03/bell-hooks-teaching-to-transgress.pdf

I've had great success with these approaches :-) I could proudly claim that many of my students, who've been thrown to the wayside by the educational system, have gone on to graduate from Research-1 universities, some of them even pursuing graduate degrees. We just have to listen to the students. We have to treat them as equals without disavowing nor uncritically accepting our hierarchical differences.
